lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.unitTitle: PF6 — Protecting and Insuring: Risk Management Across a Household
lessonRef.title: Synthesis and review: self-insuring through reserves versus buying coverage

focus: self-insuring through reserves versus buying coverage
objective: Combine the self-insurance comparison with a growing reserve to find when a fictional household could safely drop a policy, and identify what the transition depends on.
scenario: Georgiana Petrossian-Abara is planning a fictional household’s move from buying cover to carrying a risk itself. The risk, policy, and reserve figures below are invented for this exercise.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the fictional risk, policy, and reserve figures in these directions

tasks.directions: The risk is a 5% chance of a $7,600 loss in a year. The policy costs $620 a year with a $1,200 deductible. The household holds a reserve of $2,400 which grows 2.8% a year. Round to the cent.

prompts.text: What is the expected annual loss if the household carries the risk itself?
What is the expected annual cost of holding the policy, counting the premium and the expected deductible?
How much does the household save each year in expected terms by carrying the risk itself?

tasks.directions: Now follow the reserve and test when the transition becomes safe.

prompts.text: What is the $2,400 reserve worth after 5 years at 2.8% a year?
How far short of the $7,600 loss would the reserve still be after those 5 years?
If the household also set aside the $300.00 annual saving for each of the 5 years, ignoring interest on those additions, what would the reserve hold?
How far short of the $7,600 loss is that?
Can the household safely drop the policy after 5 years on these figures?
choices: Yes, the reserve covers the loss
No, the reserve is still short of the loss

prompts.text: There is a middle course: keep the policy but raise the deductible to $2,400, which the reserve already covers, cutting the premium to $455. What is the expected annual cost of that version?

tasks.directions: Answer each in a few sentences.

prompts.text: Recommend what this household should do now. Use the three options — keep the policy, drop it, or raise the deductible — and say what condition would have to be met before dropping it entirely.

The reserve grew by only $355.35 in five years while the additions contributed $1,500.00. Say what that shows about how a reserve of this size is built, and name one risk in relying on the $300.00 saving.

remediation: If the policy looks cheaper than self-insuring, check that the $1,200 deductible is being weighted by the 5% chance rather than added in full. The deductible is only paid in the years a loss occurs, so it contributes $60.00 to the expected cost and not $1,200. Write the premium as a certain cost and the deductible as a chance-weighted one before comparing anything.
extension: Find how many years of the $300.00 saving, on top of the growing reserve, would be needed before the household could absorb the whole $7,600 loss.
